system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with primary central nervous system lymphoma, ulcerative colitis, asthma, and a history of DVT/PE was admitted for her 19th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. She tolerated the treatment well with only mild nausea, which was managed with lorazepam and prochlorperazine. Methotrexate levels were monitored daily, declining to 0.14 uM by discharge, allowing safe transition home. Leucovorin rescue and sodium bicarbonate were administered as scheduled to support methotrexate clearance. Aspirin was held during admission and restarted at discharge, with heparin used for DVT prophylaxis. Liver enzymes showed mild, expected elevation, and her hemoglobin remained stable. She reported ongoing chronic right foot pain, managed with gabapentin and PRN oxycodone, and denied depressive symptoms, remaining on citalopram. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to complete three days of leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate and to continue alternating methotrexate and rituximab therapy.
problems: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Nonspecific elevation of levels of transaminase or lactic acid dehydrogenase [LDH]
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Antineoplastic and immunosuppressive drugs causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Evaluate for recurrence in a patient with CNS lymphoma, status post
resection.

TECHNIQUE:  Routine MRI examination of the brain was performed before and
after the uneventful administration of 6 mL gaobutrol intravenous contrast
material.

COMPARISON:  A series of MRIs of the brain from ___ dating back to the
earliest study from an outside facility dated ___.

FINDINGS:

There is stable encephalomalacia of the right frontal lobe, with atrophy of
the head of the caudate, insular cortex, and subcortical white matter.  There
is stable FLAIR hyperintensity surrounding the encephalomalacia.  There is a
small stable focus old blood products.  There is no abnormal contrast
enhancement or slow diffusion at this location or elsewhere in the brain. 
Scattered nonspecific foci of FLAIR hyperintensity are again seen in the
subcortical and periventricular white matter.  There is no acute infarction or
new hemorrhage. Aside from ex vacuo dilation of the frontal horn of the right
lateral ventricle, ventricular size and configuration are normal.  The
intracranial vascular flow voids of the circle of ___ and its principal
branches, as well as those of the dural venous sinuses are preserved.

Persistent frontal, sphenoid, and ethmoid sinus inflammatory disease is
present.  A mucus retention cyst is again seen in the right maxillary sinus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your oncology team members. You're here for your 20th cycle of high-dose methotrexate. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m doing okay. I’ve been feeling pretty stable since my last treatment. No headaches or weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll be giving the methotrexate tonight, starting around 11 PM. Before that, we’ll start IV fluids to help protect your kidneys and keep your urine alkaline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Last time I had some nausea with Zofran. Is that still the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, we’re switching to fosaprepitant this time. It tends to work better and causes fewer headaches than Zofran. We hope it helps you feel even better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that sounds good. I really didn’t like those headaches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your urine pH closely to make sure it stays above 8.5. That helps the methotrexate clear safely from your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when does the leucovorin start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About 24 hours after the methotrexate finishes. It helps protect your healthy cells from the chemo. We’ll give it through your port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My foot pain has been acting up a bit. Can I still take my gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. Gabapentin is safe to continue. You can also use oxycodone as needed for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my asthma inhalers—I’ve been using them as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using your albuterol and the combination inhaler as prescribed. Your breathing sounds clear today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also been on citalopram for my mood. It’s been helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important to maintain. We’ll keep it on your list. Any feelings of low mood or anxiety lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I’ve been feeling pretty steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll check your labs regularly to monitor your blood counts and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to start the methotrexate infusion now. It’ll run for about two hours. Let us know if you feel any discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready. No issues so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The infusion went smoothly. Your urine pH has stayed above 8.5, which is perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I haven’t felt nauseous at all—maybe the fosaprepitant is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll draw your first methotrexate level later today to track how it’s clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had an MRI this morning, right? Was everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the MRI showed no signs of lymphoma recurrence. The changes in your brain are stable, which is exactly what we want to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s such a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw some chronic sinus inflammation, but nothing new or concerning. It’s unrelated to your lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had sinus issues for years. Nothing to worry about, I hope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not related to your treatment. We’ll leave it to your primary doctor unless it flares up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your methotrexate level came back at 0.17 micromolar. That’s declining well, so we’re on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a safe level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s low enough that we can safely continue with leucovorin and IV fluids for a bit longer and plan for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I need to take leucovorin at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, because your level is clearing so well, you won’t need oral leucovorin or bicarbonate after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s one less thing to manage. What about aspirin? I was off it last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it during your stay for safety, but you’ll restart it at home. We used heparin for clot prevention while you were here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, because of my history with blood clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We always take extra precautions with that. Your leg has no swelling, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You tolerated everything very well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. No more IVs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll remove the IV before you leave. Just continue your regular meds, including aspirin, citalopram, gabapentin, and your inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep using oxycodone if my foot pain flares up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. And call us if you have any fever, unusual fatigue, or signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You’re doing well with your treatment. We’ll see you for your next cycle in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with primary central nervous system lymphoma was admitted for her 20th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. She reported feeling well with no neurological symptoms or systemic complaints. The chemotherapy was administered without complications, and she experienced excellent nausea control with fosaprepitant instead of her prior antiemetic. Urine alkalinization was maintained throughout, and her methotrexate level at 30 hours was 0.17 uM, indicating safe clearance. A brain MRI showed no evidence of lymphoma recurrence, with only stable chronic changes. She remained stable neurologically and hematologically, with no signs of infection or thrombosis. Aspirin was held during admission and restarted at discharge, with heparin bridging for DVT prophylaxis. She was discharged home in stable condition with no need for post-discharge leucovorin or bicarbonate, continuing her regular medications including those for chronic pain, asthma, and depression.
